title: Why worry, mind
hook: kaahe re man chitveh udam: why plot and scheme, mind, when even creatures in the rocks are fed (Gujri M5, ang 10)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the humble plea, and your line, the humble ask. Did you ask someone for help? Today, the fifth shabad of Rehras, the second in Raag Gujri, and it speaks straight to a worried mind. Day four hundred fourteen.

Two in the morning. The house is dark and everyone else is asleep, but your mind is wide awake and running scenarios. What if the job falls through. What if the test results are bad. What if I say the wrong thing tomorrow. You plan, re-plan, rehearse arguments that haven't happened. None of it changes anything at two a.m. Guru Arjan knew that mind. And he wrote it a shabad that starts with a question. Today: why worry.
screen: `2 A.M. EVERYONE ELSE ASLEEP.` → `WHAT IF, WHAT IF, WHAT IF.` → `A SHABAD FOR THE WORRIED MIND.`

segments.voice: It opens: kaahe re man chitveh udam. Why, mind, do you plot and scheme, when the dear Lord Himself has taken care of your keeping? Then the picture that gives us today's line. In rocks and stones, the shabad says in paraphrase, He created living beings, and He places their food in front of them. Think of a tiny creature living in a crack in a rock, nowhere near a field or a market, and still it's fed. Then the refrain: whoever meets the true congregation is carried across, and by the Guru's grace, even dry wood turns green. Then a harder line. Mother, father, friends, children, spouse: no one, finally, is anyone's support. The Lord provides for each and every head, so why are you afraid, mind? And another picture. A bird flies hundreds of miles, leaving its young behind. Commentators often name it the crane. Who feeds them? Who teaches them to peck? They remember her, the shabad says. It closes: all treasures and powers lie in the palm of the Lord's hand; Nanak is forever a sacrifice; You have no limit. Does this mean don't work, don't plan? No. Sikh life is built on kirat karni, honest work, and elsewhere gurbani praises effort. The word here is about the anxious scheming of a mind that thinks everything depends on it alone. Do your work. Then put the two a.m. worry down. Even the rock-creatures eat.
screen: `KAAHE RE MAN: WHY SCHEME, MIND?` · `IN THE ROCKS, FOOD PLACED BEFORE THEM.` · `A CRANE FLIES FAR; WHO FEEDS THE YOUNG?` · `WORK HONESTLY; PUT THE WORRY DOWN.` · then, large: `EVEN THE ROCK-CREATURES EAT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: put one worry down. Name one worry that's been riding with you. Hold it in your mind as if it were a stone in your hand. Feel how heavy it is. Ask: is there one honest thing I can do about this today? If yes, note it. Then picture setting the stone down on the ground beside you. It's still there. You're just not carrying it for the next two minutes. If you pray, you can say Waheguru once, and let the hand stay open. The bell holds the time.
Why worry. Kaahe re man chitveh udam: Guru Arjan asks the anxious mind why it schemes, when even creatures in the rocks are given their food.
Your line: even the rock-creatures eat. Tonight, if worry wakes you, do the one honest thing you can, or note it for morning, then set the stone down. Day four hundred fourteen.

howItsDone: Kaahe re man chitveh udam is the fifth shabad of Rehras Sahib, recited each evening; Sikhs pair its trust in the Lord's provision with kirat karni, earning an honest living.

original.note: Gurmukhi: rijak, sustenance, daily bread; the Lord places it before even the creatures in the rocks.

trapdoor: what you thought: why worry, mind is a cheerful don't-worry-be-happy.
what it means: a mind that thinks everything depends on it alone is asked to trust the One who feeds every creature.
what a scholar hears: udam in this line means anxious scheming, while elsewhere gurbani praises udam as effort; the crane image draws on a familiar picture of migrating birds in Punjabi poetry.
